reason: Hilbert is a 27-person, $28M a16z Series A AI growth platform whose live ATS feed shows delivery scaling one-for-one with headcount - vertical-specific human operators (AI Growth Architect, AI Growth Architect - Fashion, Growth Operator - Grocery/QSR/Retail, Forward Deployed Data Engineer (Integration)) hired to be, in the posting's own words, the product's "most demanding internal user, finding where the product's reasoning breaks down" - which is exactly the human-delivered-to-AI-product transition and evaluation-harness gap Daniel Kirichanski fixes.

company.name: Hilbert (Hilbert AI Co.)
company.one_liner: Agentic, data-science-first growth infrastructure that turns fragmented B2C customer data into predictive insight and automated growth actions via natural language, used by Walmart, FreshDirect, Blank Street and Levain Bakery.
company.industry: AI / growth analytics software for B2C brands and Fortune 500 enterprises
company.stage: Series A - $28M led by Andreessen Horowitz (announced 2026-04-15), also Asylum Ventures; ~27 employees (+480% YoY), distributed across US, Turkey, Netherlands, Spain, Germany

evidence_jobs.title: AI Growth Architect
evidence_jobs.quote: You run Hilbert on live growth problems, identify where its reasoning can do better, and translate those findings into structured input

evidence_jobs.title: AI Engineer - Core
evidence_jobs.quote: You'll own core pieces of the AI stack that power Hilbert's demand intelligence platform - designing agent architectures, building evaluation systems, and making hard tradeoffs between accuracy, latency, and cost in production.

evidence_jobs.title: Product Manager, Growth
evidence_jobs.quote: A small, select group of growth operators sit at the core of our company. These minds shape how Hilbert's intelligence layer evolves, how customers grow, and how the company goes to market.

people_spec: Co-Founder, Engineering (Hilbert has no CTO, VP Engineering, or Head of Platform/Infrastructure - engineering is owned by a co-founder, so this is the seat that owns cost-to-deliver)
talk_track: I spend my time moving work that lives in people's hands into AI systems that hold up under real load - platform engineering at PayPal and Ripple, then AI agents running incident response at Tricentis. Your AI Growth Architect posting says the hire will "run Hilbert on live growth problems, identify where its reasoning can do better, and translate those findings into structured input," and it sits on the careers page next to AI Growth Architect - Fashion, Growth Operator - Grocery/QSR & Retail, and a Forward Deployed Data Engineer (Integration). Read together, those four are one pattern: right now each new vertical costs a person, because the evaluation harness and the ingestion layer still live in human heads rather than in the product. That is the quietest way gross margin disappears after a Series A - cost-to-deliver rises with revenue instead of flattening, and it usually shows up two quarters after the headcount does. The durable fix is capturing what those architects learn as evals and memory the platform owns, so vertical five costs a config change instead of a hire. Which vertical do you think breaks the pattern first? - Daniel Kirichanski, Prime Path Global
